doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Street-corner kids and Trombone Shorty
summary: Neighbourhood elders teach children by ear; she recalls hearing child Troy Andrews and a band of boys outside the Cathedral.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: No, no, no. You said that very well. My wife and I were in New Orleans just about a year ago. And we were walking I think on Canal Street I guess, and we could hear this sound of this band and we literally followed the sound. And then on the corner of I guess Bourbon Street there was this group of young kids playing. And they were unbelievable. You couldn’t possibly write down what they were playing. And I just thought that was a joy to see, that that still goes on. Is there any organization to that kind of street corner playing that you’re aware of? Is there a hierarchy or something in how that happens?

I don’t know. Let me put it this way. It’s just that this guy says to this child, “Take this horn and I’m going to teach you how to play this, I’m going to teach you how to play that.” And the little child struggles with it and finally he learns how to play and then you get another kid together. You know it’s coming out of the neighborhoods. It’s coming out of the neighborhoods. And it’s not necessarily that you’re teaching them to read at that point, it’s just teaching them to respond to what’s naturally within. And we have many, many, many musicians who started that way, little ones, they say, young men — what’s this child’s name now — Troy Andrews.
Oh, the “Trombone Shorty” they call him.

Yes. “Trombone Shorty.” Okay now the trombone was bigger than he was when he started playing and he was maybe about that tall but he was playing that horn and he was getting this big sound. I remember I used to sing with the St. Louis Cathedral Choir. And we’d do a ten o’clock mass at the Cathedral. And one Sunday I came out of mass and I

heard this music but I didn’t see these people. And I went to the corner and it’s all these little boys, little boys. Trombone Shorty with the trombone and a little kid with the trumpet. And I imagine they were like nine, ten years old. There was a whole band of these kids. I got so excited I ran inside to the rectory and I said, “You guys got to come out here and see this.” And I think that the older gentlemen, the older players, just sort of took them in hand and said okay learn these songs, learn these songs. And these kids just started playing and playing and finally they got into where they were going to the training, they got into the formal bit, but they never lost, they never lost that root thing. They never lost that feeling, that spirit. No matter what they play. No matter what they play. Whether they’re playing the traditional or they’re playing the blues or they’re playing straight ahead jazz or whatever, that feeling is still there.
This group I mentioned started playing “Stand By Me,” you know? And what they did with it was indescribable. But it was so great, and they just went on forever — the endurance even, wow.
